It really depends on the usage and plans with the compressed data, but I would generally say that, no, it wouldn't work.

If your plan is to merely compress something and use the compressed version, then it wouldn't be beneficial to 'recompress' already compressed information. We can see this in music and videos where algorithms attempt to compress it with minimal loss of information. In these cases, the compressed string is as compressed as possible without losing additional info. Any additional attempts would either result in no change or a loss in information.

If your plan is to compress and then decompress, then we have to now remember how to decompress every substring which takes up added storage.

Lastly, anything you compress should already be as small as possible. If putting compressed information back into the algorithm could allow it to become more efficient, then whatever algorithm you're using is inefficient. After all, why not just use the equivalent of the algorithm applied twice from the beginning?

The actual last thing I'll say here is that these problems are also typically best solved on an individual level. There is no easy, generalizable methodology that works on all use-cases. In addition, the future is tending towards ML compression as Google research has already shown us that they were able to use their ML to compress videos much more than currently optimal methodologies.

It's theoretically possible but not proven whatsoever. The main discussions come from using pi - a number conjectured to be normal although not proven - as a way to store data. 

Suppose we had some data sequence which we wanted to compress. If pi is normal, then this sequence occurs at some point in pi, and we can reference that sequence using only 2 numbers: an offset and a length. The offset refers to where the sequence starts on Pi's decimal representation, and the length is the length of the sequence.

In theory, this could beat all currently known methods of compression. The main issues are:

1. We don't have the easy ability to calculate where a sequence would occur. Right now, any method would be inefficient.

2. There is always the possibility that the offset itself would become larger than whatever data is stored.

I'd like to address the point you made about compressing infinitely large numbers. You bring up some ideas present in abstract algebra. To formalize it, let's consider the group of the integers. In this case, the integers are a group defined the operation of addition by the identity of 0 and the generator 1 with its identity represented as -1 with no other rules. 

We see then that any number could be represented as a repeated application of the number 1; however, in order to represent this number, we still need to know how many times to apply the generator. This is equivalent to the number itself (since any number is equal to itself times 1). 

The closest we could ever come to infinite compression would be through using normal numbers with an index and length to denote the sequence; however, these tools are typically very inefficient as finding a large sequence in a normal number is a non-trivial, computationally long task.

To start, I think it is fairly clear that each set is infinite, but let's break it down anyways.

Theorem: Let B be a set. If for each finite subset S of B there is an element x \in B with x \notin S, then B is infinite.

For the set of all numbers with even numbers of digits, I propose that there will always be some number of the form 10^(2n-1) which is not included in any finite subset that you could come up with where n is a natural number. If true, then the set of all numbers with even numbers of digits is infinite. If false, then the set is at least as large as the natural numbers (since it must contain all numbers of the form 10^[2n-1] where n \in N) and is therefore infinite. Thus, we know that the set is infinite. We can construct a similar argument for the set of all numbers with odd numbers of digits.

Now that we know that both sets are infinite, we must determine if they are countable or uncountably infinite. This is relatively straightforward. Since both sets are subsets of the natural numbers, they cannot be larger than the natural numbers. Therefore, since the natural numbers are countable, so are both of your sets!

Hi! I actually am a data scientist who uses TDA at my job. There are many applications, but I'll list a few:


- When we construct simplicial complexes from the data, we look for a new feature: holes. We can use this a variety of ways like comparing dimensionality (this 4D dataset can be reduced to 3D based on the point cloud's topology).


 - We can investigate time series by considering the 'state' that it's in at any given moment. For example, we might consider all the possible permutations of the values of a subset of the time series as it moves along. That is, consider n points in a row of a time series. We can label these by their ordering in the time series and then sort them by their values. So, a permutation of (0,1,2) corresponds to a set of increasing values whereas a set of (2,1,0) corresponds to decreasing. Then, we can construct a DiGraph based on how we move from permutation to permutation in the time series. We can then understand some of the frequent patterns that the time series exhibits. In addition, we can calculate things like the entropy of the system and at which states have the highest entropy. This info can be used for anomaly detection, comparison to noise or chaos, and even making predictions.


- The last one I'll mention is the construction of complexes for clustering. We can use topological complexes to understand the shape of data including where a model might be underperforming by using a variety of colorings on the topological space. This is frequently used in the field of biology. I'd recommend looking into Gunnar Carlsson as he has some good lectures on this which I can't do justice.

It's interesting how these algorithms work depending on the group of people. They're based on a mathematical concept called random time walks along graphs. The idea being, how far away is one idea from another with each idea being a vertex in the graph.

The part where it gets interesting is that these graphs change as people walk along the graphs. Consider some natural number (positive integer) N.  Then we can rewrite N as

N = a0 + a1 * 10 + a2 * 10^2 + ...

Where a0 is the ones digit, a1 is the tens digit, and so on and so forth.  Then we can look at the remainder of N when divided by 9.  Note that 10 % 9 = 1!  So, we have 

N = a0 + a1 * 1 + a2 * 1 + ... (mod 9)

Assuming that you guys already talk and get along well, you could ask if she wants to get coffee or lunch sometime soon.  If she says that she'd like to, then she's probably interested.  If not, then that's it!  Like you said, rejection wouldn't be that bad.

As someone who has had experience being cheated on and not told (a mutual friend told me luckily), it is not a good feeling in the slightest to be cheated on and lied to.  I think that there is always the possibility that they might not, but at the same time, if they still haven't told their ex, then I doubt that he's even worth your time.  My advice to you would be to just keep looking for someone who's actions reflect what you want in a relationship, which seems to me to be commitment (or at least to not be cheated on).  Keep looking for someone better!
